lead: A spring pulls or pushes a mass back toward equilibrium, so the mass overshoots and repeats the same motion. This back-and-forth is mechanical vibration. When the restoring force is proportional to displacement, the motion is simple harmonic motion (SHM). Its natural angular frequency depends only on stiffness k and mass m. The same mathematics describes a car on its suspension, a building in an earthquake, and a quartz watch crystal. This chapter covers free undamped vibration: the mass oscillates with no friction and no outside pushing.
prereq: You need: Newton's second law and spring force F = −kx from Unit 5, and the force–acceleration relation from 6.5.

sections.h3: Simple harmonic motion and a spring

blocks.text: Simple harmonic motion is motion in which the acceleration is proportional to displacement from equilibrium and directed opposite to it. The standard displacement equation is:

blocks.where: x is displacement from equilibrium in m; A is amplitude in m; ω_n is natural angular frequency in rad/s; t is time in s; φ is phase angle in rad.

blocks.text: The subscript n marks the natural frequency: the frequency the system has when left alone. For a mass m on a spring of stiffness k, put the spring force into Newton's second law.

items: Write the force on the mass: F = −k x. The minus sign means the force points back toward equilibrium.
Use Newton's second law: m a = −k x.
Replace acceleration by the second derivative of displacement: m d²x/dt² = −k x.
Compare with the SHM condition a = −ω_n² x. This gives ω_n² = k/m.

blocks.where: ω_n is natural angular frequency in rad/s; k is spring stiffness in N/m; m is mass in kg.

blocks.text: The period T is the time for one full cycle. Frequency f is the number of cycles per second.

blocks.where: T is period in s; f is frequency in Hz; ω_n is natural angular frequency in rad/s; π ≈ 3.1416.

items: More mass gives lower ω_n and longer period.
A stiffer spring gives higher ω_n and shorter period.
In linear SHM, amplitude A does not change ω_n or T.
For a hanging mass, gravity only shifts the equilibrium position. The oscillation frequency is still √(k/m).

blocks.text: Some syllabi call this free vibration or mechanical vibrations.
Differentiate displacement once for velocity and twice for acceleration.
v = dx/dt = Aω_n cos(ω_n t + φ),   a = dv/dt = −Aω_n² sin(ω_n t + φ) = −ω_n² x
blocks.where: v is velocity in m/s; a is acceleration in m/s²; A is amplitude in m; ω_n is natural angular frequency in rad/s; x is displacement in m.

blocks.text: At equilibrium, x = 0. Speed is maximum there, v_max = Aω_n, and acceleration is zero. At the extremes, x = ±A. Speed is zero there, and acceleration has maximum magnitude a_max = Aω_n², pointing toward equilibrium.
The phase φ sets the starting point. Pull down and release from rest: x = A cos(ω_n t) if down is positive. Push through equilibrium at t = 0: x = A sin(ω_n t). Both choices have the same ω_n and T.
ω_n is in rad/s. Frequency f is in Hz (cycles per second). They are linked by ω_n = 2πf, so f = 1 Hz corresponds to ω_n = 2π rad/s. Period T is in s. Never quote ω_n as a frequency in Hz.
Convert stiffness before substituting. 1 N/cm = 100 N/m, and 1 N/mm = 1000 N/m. A spring rated 8 N/cm is k = 800 N/m.

Free vibration ignores friction. Real systems have damping, which slowly reduces amplitude. Forced vibration near the natural frequency causes resonance, where a small periodic force can build a large amplitude. Damped and forced vibration are beyond this chapter.
For rotational vibration, mass moment of inertia replaces mass. Use Unit 4 for I, and 6.7 for an energy check.

figure.caption: Generic simple harmonic motion that starts at equilibrium: x = 0.05 sin(20t). Amplitude 0.05 m, ω_n = 20 rad/s, one complete cycle in about 0.314 s.

spec.aria: A sinusoidal displacement-time graph for a 0.05 m amplitude and 20 rad/s angular frequency.

examples.question: A 2.0 kg mass hangs on a spring of stiffness k = 800 N/m. It is pulled down 0.05 m from equilibrium and released from rest. Find the angular frequency, period, frequency and maximum speed.
steps: List the data: m = 2.0 kg, k = 800 N/m, A = 0.05 m. The release is from rest at the pulled position, so this position is an extreme and A is the amplitude.
Find period: T = 2π/ω_n = 2π/20 = π/10 = 0.314 s to three significant figures.
Find frequency: f = 1/T = 1/0.314 = 3.18 Hz. Equivalently, f = ω_n/(2π) = 20/(2π) = 3.18 Hz.
Maximum speed occurs at equilibrium: v_max = Aω_n = 0.05 × 20 = 1.0 m/s.
The hanging weight only shifts equilibrium downward. It does not change ω_n, T, f or v_max.
examples.answer: ω_n = 20 rad/s, T = 0.314 s, f = 3.18 Hz and v_max = 1.0 m/s.
examples.check:
import math
m = 2.0
k = 800.0
A = 0.05
w = math.sqrt(k / m)
T = 2.0 * math.pi / w
f = 1.0 / T
vmax = A * w
print(round(w, 1))
print(round(T, 3))
print(round(f, 2))
print(round(vmax, 1))

traps: Mixing ω_n in rad/s with f in Hz. A value of 20 rad/s is about 3.18 Hz, not 20 Hz.
Using k in N/cm without converting. 8 N/cm is 800 N/m. If you substitute k = 8, you are out by a factor of 100 in k, so ω_n (and f) comes out 10 times too small.
Writing T = 1/ω_n instead of T = 2π/ω_n. The factor 2π is the common lost mark.
Thinking a larger amplitude changes the natural frequency of a linear spring-mass system. It does not.
Getting the sign of acceleration wrong. In SHM, a = −ω_n² x always points toward equilibrium, opposite to x.

quiz.q: Define simple harmonic motion and write its acceleration condition.
quiz.a: Acceleration is proportional to displacement from equilibrium and opposite in direction: a = −ω_n² x. The displacement is x = A sin(ω_n t + φ).

quiz.q: Give the SI units of ω_n, f and T.
quiz.a: ω_n is in rad/s, f is in Hz (cycles/s), and T is in s.

quiz.q: Why is the natural frequency of a mass on a spring independent of amplitude?
quiz.a: The restoring force is F = −kx, proportional to x. Newton's second law gives a = −(k/m)x. Comparing with a = −ω_n²x gives ω_n = √(k/m). Amplitude cancels out, so ω_n does not depend on A.

quiz.q: A 0.50 kg mass is on a spring of stiffness 200 N/m. Find ω_n, T and f.
In SHM with amplitude 0.020 m and ω_n = 10 rad/s, find the maximum speed and maximum acceleration magnitude.
A spring-mass system has stiffness k and mass m. If k is made four times larger and m is made two times larger, how do ω_n and T change?
quiz.a: New ω_n = √(4k / 2m) = √2 × √(k/m). So ω_n increases by a factor √2 ≈ 1.41. T = 2π/ω_n, so T decreases by a factor √2 ≈ 0.707.

quiz.q: At which positions in SHM are speed and acceleration maximum? Explain using x.
quiz.a: At equilibrium x = 0, speed is maximum (Aω_n) and acceleration is zero. At extremes x = ±A, speed is zero and acceleration magnitude is maximum (Aω_n²), directed toward equilibrium.

quiz.q: Why does gravity not change the frequency of a hanging spring-mass system?
quiz.a: The constant weight shifts the equilibrium position downward. About that new equilibrium, the extra force is still −kx, so ω_n = √(k/m) is unchanged.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real machines need vibration control: engine mounts, washing-machine suspensions and building dampers are designed so their natural frequencies stay away from operating speeds. MEMS accelerometers in phones use tiny vibrating masses to sense motion. Wind turbines and bridges are monitored for changes in natural frequency that signal stiffness loss. Search "single degree of freedom vibration", "natural frequency" and "damping ratio" for the next step.
